This whole narrative is built on finding the few examples when automation didn't result in a job loss, while completely ignoring the numerous cases when it did. The problem is, we're not just automating some labor this time. We're automating minds, minds that can potentially perform any labor, if given proper physical capabilities. And it will do it at a fraction of a cost, 10-1000x faster, 24/7, fewer errors, no sick days. It's already happening in IT: junior developers can't find jobs. It's also happening with drivers - we're in the middle of taxi drivers being replaced. And what is this magical source of new jobs for the ~5 million US taxi drivers? Can you name it? Doubt it. AI can and will take your job. It's inevitable. The question is only when.

<sigh> This assumption that the creation of new jobs will continue as automation sophistication improves is an unwarranted extension of prior trends. Eliminating almost all farmers wiped out some 90% of all labor in that era - but didn't wipe out many *potential* jobs, because there were thousands of categories of more complex work that could not be done by a tractor - tractors are neither smart nor particularly dextrous. What it did was free up people who could then be tasked to do those more complex forms of work, mostly in factories, and eventually in services as our economy evolved. But even casual examination shows you that's not an indefinite trend. As the sophistication of automation increases, it overlaps a larger percentage of not just EXISTING jobs, but also POTENTIAL jobs. The difference being, that if you come up with a new form of low to medium complexity job to replace the one you lost, it can be almost immediately automated away again because it's now easy to teach an AI or build a robot to do that new job instead. You have to come up with increasingly complex and abstract tasks for humans to do that automation cannot - until you run out of track. Human capability is limited. We are not all Einstein, and even if we were, we are discussing building AI that is smarter than he was. You will not be able to come up with a form of work that is so complex and sophisticated that a machine cannot learn it in short order. At that point there will in fact be no new jobs. We will have hit the end of the runway and found that it opens into a yawning chasm of economic irrelevance.

What would your advice be to someone who is in their 40s, working full time at a non-coding job, and working on a Computer Science degree via evening classes? I think the advice of finding bigger projects and doing coding challenges is excellent and it makes sense, but at the same time I feel like I literally don't have the free time needed to do such things until I'm done with school. I work during the day, I have classes two nights a week, and then the rest of the time is usually dedicated to studying and doing assignments for school. Once school is over, I could see having plenty of time to dive into projects and challenges to try and keep from losing everything I learned, but it feels like that would also mean that there could be some lag time between graduating and actually being "ready" to try for a different job. I suppose the good thing about that is that I don't hate my current job. It's just that my current job isn't at all computer science related, so I of course want to eventually move on to something that is related so that all this schooling hasn't been for nothing.
